name: EmCyte PurePRP

card.summary: A point-of-care centrifuge kit that concentrates platelets from a patient's own blood into leukocyte-poor platelet-rich plasma, which clinics use for facial skin rejuvenation treatments such as PRP facials and microneedling.
card.note: A clinic-used medical device; PRP treatments are generally off-label and results vary between patients.

quick.overview:
EmCyte PurePRP is a commercial system for preparing platelet-rich plasma (PRP) at the point of care. Blood is drawn from the patient, spun in a centrifuge and concentrated into a platelet-rich preparation that is low in white blood cells (a 'neutrophil-poor' or leukocyte-poor PRP). Clinics use PRP for skin rejuvenation and hair loss, including in 'vampire facials' with microneedling.

For appearance, the claimed effect is better skin texture, fewer fine lines and more even tone. In a small 2019 study of 11 volunteers who received three PurePRP injection sessions, researchers reported reductions in brown spots and wrinkles, improved firmness and reduced redness measured by biometric instruments.
quick.how: The kit is used by a clinician, not by consumers. A blood sample is processed in a centrifuge with the kit's disposable components, and the resulting PRP is injected or applied with microneedling in facial treatments, typically in a series of sessions. The same systems are also used in orthopedic care.
quick.risks: PRP is made from the patient's own blood, so allergic reactions are uncommon, but injections can cause bruising, swelling and infection risks, and treatments done in unlicensed settings with shared equipment have caused harm; the CDC linked three HIV diagnoses to a New Mexico spa. The FDA clears the preparation devices but does not regulate PRP itself, so cosmetic use is off-label. Results and PRP composition differ between systems and patients.

lead: EmCyte PurePRP is a family of point-of-care kits (including the PurePRP II 60-mL kit) that concentrate platelets from a patient's blood into platelet-rich plasma (PRP) [4]. Wikipedia describes PRP as a concentrate of a person's own plasma in which red cells are removed and platelets kept, made with commercial kits and a centrifuge, aiming for roughly 3 to 5 times normal platelet levels [5].

Clinics use PRP in orthopedics, in hair loss treatment and for skin: injected to reduce wrinkles and blemishes, often with microneedling in 'vampire facials' [5]. In a 2019 clinical study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology, the EmCyte PurePRP system was used to produce neutrophil-poor PRP for facial rejuvenation. Eleven volunteers received three treatments, and instrumental measures showed significant reductions in brown spot counts and area, wrinkles and redness, and improved firmness [2].

Researchers have compared commercial PRP systems and found they differ in cell composition: one study compared five systems including the Emcyte Genesis CS [3], and a retrospective analysis checked whether the PurePRP II 60-mL kit returned the content the manufacturer expects in routine clinical care [4]. A scoping review of point-of-care PRP devices describes the field's growth and differences between devices [1].

chain: Patient's blood is drawn and centrifuged in the kit
Injected or applied with microneedling to the face
Skin texture, tone and firmness may improve
angle.text: The kit produces the PRP that clinicians use in facial rejuvenation. In a small study of its output, volunteers showed fewer brown spots and wrinkles and better firmness on instrumental measurement.

infobox: Device clearance for preparation kits; PRP use is typically off-label

paras: PRP is prepared by drawing blood, spinning it in a centrifuge to separate plasma, platelets and red cells, and keeping a platelet-rich fraction; the resulting concentrate varies by person and facility [5]. Platelets release growth factors and cytokines that may support healing [5].

PurePRP is described in the literature as producing a PRP that excludes granulocytes and has low hematocrit, with the manufacturer's protocols varying in how the output is configured [4]. Systems differ: a 2017 comparison of five commercial separation systems found differences in cellular composition and pH [3].

PRP is used in dermatology and cosmetic practice for skin rejuvenation, hair loss and scars, sometimes combined with microneedling in so-called vampire facials [5]. The 2019 PurePRP facial rejuvenation study measured brown spots, wrinkles, firmness and redness before and after three treatments and at six-month follow-up [2].

According to Wikipedia, the FDA does not regulate PRP itself, so clinical use is off-label, though the devices that prepare it require clearance [5]. Adverse effects are generally low, but in 2024 the CDC linked three HIV diagnoses to an unlicensed New Mexico spa that reused blood-contaminated equipment [5].

A 2019 clinical trial of autologous PurePRP injections for facial skin rejuvenation enrolled 11 volunteers who received three treatments; brown spot count and area, wrinkle count and volume, and skin redness decreased significantly and firmness improved, with patient self-assessment also collected [2]. It was small and did not report a control group in the abstract available. A retrospective analysis of the PurePRP II 60-mL kit in routine clinical use examined whether its output matched the manufacturer's expectations [4]. Comparative laboratory work shows composition differs between commercial PRP systems [3].
